The breeding biology of Providence petrel (Pterodroma solandri) has been studied primarily on Lord Howe Island, where the species forms dense colonies on the island's montane slopes. Under the thermal conditions typical of an actively incubating adult (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), females produce a single egg per nesting attempt [N_R_i = single egg per nesting attempt], and available data suggest they typically raise only one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year], a pattern consistent with the slow reproductive tempo characteristic of many procellariiform seabirds. This maximum reproductive output reflects the high energetic burden of provisioning a single, slowly developing chick. Incubation itself, which is shared by both parents, lasts approximately 55 days [ab = approximately 55 days] and occurs at a nest cavity temperature of around 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a regime that balances embryonic development with the need to minimize water loss from the porous eggshell. Hatchlings emerge at a very modest wet weight of approximately 50 grams [Wwb = approximately 50 grams], a value derived from studies of the closely related Pterodroma macroptera and provisionally applied here in the absence of direct measurements for P. solandri.

During the prolonged nestling phase, developing chicks undergo a remarkable transformation, more than decupling their birth mass as they accumulate the lipid reserves necessary for a successful fledging. The asymptotic wet weight attained by nestlings prior to fledging is roughly 610 grams [Wwi = roughly 610 grams], a value that represents the ultimate mass achieved after approximately nine weeks of continuous parental provisioning. This adult-sized mass is reached while the chick's body temperature is maintained near the adult active level of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], a homeothermic condition that the nestling attains gradually after the initial brooding period. The period from hatching to the achievement of this asymptotic mass serves as a critical developmental window, during which the chick transitions from receiving periodic meals to enduring longer intervals between feeds as the parents undertake increasingly distant foraging trips. Nestlings that fail to reach this threshold mass before nest departure face substantially reduced post-fledging survival probabilities.

Under the standard active body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], field observations indicate that fledging, marked by the chick's first sustained flight and departure from the burrow, occurs at approximately 109 days after hatching [tx = approximately 109 days after hatching]. This developmental schedule is notably prolonged compared to many smaller procellariids, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a lipid-rich but calorically dilute diet of squid and crustaceans. Following fledging, young birds embark on an extended pelagic phase, during which they develop foraging proficiency and accumulate the somatic reserves necessary to support the onset of reproductive function. Based on observations of the congeneric Pterodroma macroptera, gonadal maturity is estimated at approximately 327 days after hatching [tp = approximately 327 days after hatching], though direct measurements for P at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. solandri are lacking.

The transition from immaturity to active breeding is not immediate upon reaching sexual maturity, as first-time breeders face substantial delays related to territory acquisition and mate selection. The time elapsed since birth at first brood, representing the age at which a pair successfully produces its first egg, is approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days] under the thermal conditions typical of the species (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]). This two-year delay between fledging and first breeding is intermediate among gadfly petrels, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and deferred reproduction over early breeding. This extended pre-reproductive period allows young birds to refine their foraging skills, establish stable pair bonds, and secure a suitable nest cavity in the competitive colonial environment. Not all adults breed every year; in some seasons, particularly following poor oceanographic conditions, a substantial proportion of the population may skip reproduction entirely, further depressing the already low annual recruitment rate of new breeders into the colony.

At an active body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], long-term banding studies on Lord Howe Island have provided valuable data on the species' maximum longevity, revealing that the oldest documented individuals survive for approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years]. Some records, however, suggest that individuals may occasionally exceed 30 years [am = 30 years], a lifespan that places Pterodroma solandri among the longer-lived members of its genus. This extreme longevity, combined with an exceptionally low annual reproductive output of approximately one egg per year [Ri = approximately one egg per year] and a single nesting attempt per breeding season [F_R_i = single nesting attempt per breeding season], exemplifies a classic slow life-history strategy. Such a strategy is highly sensitive to adult mortality rates; even small increases in mortality from introduced predators or incidental bycatch in fisheries can drive rapid population declines, as the species lacks the compensatory reproductive capacity to offset the loss of long-lived adults. The ongoing recovery of the Lord Howe Island population following the successful eradication of invasive rodents underscores the critical importance of safeguarding adult survival for the persistence of this species.
